candidateRows: Paul's received tradition in 1 Corinthians 15 preserves an early historical proclamation that Christ was buried, raised, and seen by numerous witnesses.
The asserted early transmission and named appearances provide a principal historical foundation for the affirmative bodily-resurrection case.
After stating his traditional approach, Albrecht introduces Paul's received proclamation and argues that it circulated through the churches before being recorded.
Paul's language about Christ's glorious body and Acts' contrast between David's occupied tomb and Christ's uncorrupted flesh support a bodily resurrection and empty tomb.
This move directly addresses the disputed bodily character of the resurrection through textual claims about body, flesh, corruption, and the tomb.
Albrecht turns from the transmitted proclamation to the manner of resurrection, joining Philippians' glorious-body language to Peter's sermon in Acts.
Independent New Testament accounts of appearances to Peter, the women, the disciples, and Thomas provide multiple attestation for Jesus' bodily appearances.
Multiple attestation of named postmortem appearances is presented as a major historical reason to accept the resurrection testimony.
Following the empty-tomb argument, Albrecht surveys appearance traditions across Paul and several Gospels and stresses their distinct authorial forms.
Even skeptical scholars concede that disciples experienced or believed they saw the risen Jesus, while the sources give no indication that the appearances were merely visions.
The move uses concessions from nonbelieving scholars and the disciples' costly commitment to resist non-bodily explanations of the appearances.
Albrecht contrasts his reliance on traditional sources with concessions attributed to skeptical scholars, then connects the disciples' conviction to martyrdom.
Early church writers linked to apostolic witnesses consistently taught that Christ rose in flesh, preserving an unbroken chain of bodily-resurrection testimony.
The claimed proximity of these writers to apostles and eyewitnesses is offered as an independent transmission chain for the bodily-resurrection belief.
After discussing New Testament testimony, Albrecht appeals to Clement, Ignatius, Irenaeus, and Polycarp as early custodians of apostolic teaching.
Believing apologists often begin from non-inductive commitments, whereas historians must use inductive methods and keep every conclusion tentative and revisable.
This methodological distinction challenges the historical force of a resurrection case built after religious commitment rather than from revisable inference.
Albrecht's presentation of Christian sources as affirmative historical evidence for bodily resurrection.
After explaining his background, Price argues that apologetic reasoning commonly follows conversion and contrasts it with provisional historical inquiry.
Historical judgment depends on analogy with present experience; because resurrections lack credible modern analogues but resemble ancient myths, Jesus' resurrection is historically improbable.
The move supplies Price's principal reason for a negative historical verdict on the motion while stopping short of claiming certainty that resurrection is impossible.
Albrecht's treatment of ancient resurrection narratives and appearances as sufficient historical testimony.
Price explains the principle of analogy with extraordinary-claim examples, then compares resurrection reports with modern experience and ancient religious narratives.
Divine ability can make a miracle possible without showing that it occurred, and faith cannot substitute for historical grounds for believing Jesus rose.
The distinction between possibility and occurrence directly blocks an appeal to divine power from establishing the debated historical event.
The believer's contention that divine involvement overcomes the antecedent improbability of a resurrection.
Near the end of his opening, Price grants that God could perform improbable acts but demands an epistemic basis beyond faith for concluding one occurred.
Attis has pre-Christian evidence suggestive of resurrection, while other pagan resurrection narratives clearly predate Christianity.
The claim supplies historical-analogy evidence for Price's challenge to the alleged uniqueness and evidential force of the Christian resurrection tradition.
Albrecht's contention that the earliest Attis evidence contains no resurrection account and that such readings are later.
During Albrecht's cross-examination, Price cites an Attis image and then broadens the answer to Osiris and Baal as resurrection traditions predating Jesus.
The Attis case lacks early documentary testimony to a resurrection, leaving only an ambiguous pottery depiction and later writings.
This challenges the chronological and documentary foundation of a principal pagan parallel offered against the uniqueness of Jesus' resurrection.
Price's appeal to an early pottery depiction and later Attis documents as evidence of a resurrection tradition.
Albrecht distinguishes visual interpretation from written attestation and obtains Price's acknowledgment that he has not found an early writing describing Attis's resurrection.
Osiris is plainly restored from death, fathers Horus, and then rules the netherworld, making his story analogous to Jesus' resurrection and exaltation.
The argument presents a concrete pre-Christian resurrection analogue intended to undermine claims that the Christian narrative is historically unique.
Albrecht's observation that scholars are divided over whether Osiris can properly be said to have resurrected.
Price argues that Isis reassembled and revived the dismembered Osiris, after which Osiris entered the underworld as lord and judge, paralleling Christian claims.
The Osiris text itself says he did not die, so the fantasy narrative and divided scholarship do not establish a clear resurrection parallel.
The argument directly contests whether Price's chief pagan analogue belongs in the same evidential category as a death followed by bodily resurrection.
Price's claim that Osiris was raised from the dead after Isis reassembled and anointed his severed body.
Albrecht stresses the formula saying Osiris had not died, the fantastic character of the tale, and scholarly disagreement before Price rejects the requested concession.
New Ugaritic evidence supports Baal's death and resurrection, while early Christian explanations presuppose acknowledged pagan dying-and-rising traditions.
This combines primary-tradition chronology with early Christian reception evidence to defend pagan precedents against the Christian-uniqueness objection.
Albrecht's claim that the Baal narrative has serious gaps and that scholars deny Baal underwent resurrection.
Price invokes newer texts said to confirm Baal's death and return, then argues that fathers would not posit satanic advance counterfeiting unless such parallels were recognized.
Justin Martyr neither dates pagan resurrection tales before Christianity nor treats their endings as equivalent to Christ's unique death and resurrection.
The argument attacks Price's use of an early Christian witness as evidence that pre-Christian resurrection parallels were already historically established.
Price's appeal to early fathers who explained pagan dying-and-rising gods as satanic counterfeits made in advance.
Albrecht argues that Justin describes pagan imitation rather than priority, emphasizes differences in suffering and death, and claims no relevant evidence predates Christianity.
First Corinthians 15 conflicts with Galatians because one depicts Paul receiving the gospel through transmission while the other denies any mortal source.
The argument challenges the coherence and authorship of a foundational early source commonly used to establish resurrection appearances and tradition.
Albrecht's request for Price to justify his position that the First Corinthians 15 account is unreliable.
Price contrasts Paul's claim of direct revelation in Galatians with the delivered tradition in First Corinthians 15 and questions whether one writer produced both passages.
Albrecht uncritically assumes disputed authorship and authenticity for New Testament and patristic documents, treating church tradition as critical history.
The objection targets the provenance and historical reliability of the documentary foundation on which Albrecht builds the bodily-resurrection case.
Albrecht's reliance on attributed New Testament, apostolic-father, and later church testimony as a coherent historical chain.
At the opening of his cross-examination, Price argues that serious authorship doubts surround the sources and that Albrecht substitutes an authorized church account for critical analysis.
First Corinthians 15 supports an early spiritual rather than physical resurrection and directly conflicts with Luke's insistence on flesh and bones.
The claim directly contests the motion by arguing that a foundational early Christian source teaches a nonphysical resurrection rather than bodily revival.
Albrecht's contention that the earliest Christians believed Christ bodily rose from the dead.
Price reads flesh and blood and the spiritual body in Paul as nonphysical, then contrasts that account with Luke's denial that the risen Jesus is a spirit.
Paul's term for spiritual does not mean immaterial, as Pauline usage and Ignatius show that fleshly and spiritual predicates can coexist.
The linguistic argument directly defends bodily resurrection by denying that Paul's description of a spiritual body excludes transformed physical embodiment.
Price's interpretation of Paul's spiritual and incorruptible body as necessarily nonfleshly and nonphysical.
Albrecht argues from ancient rather than modern semantic usage, cites consistent Pauline usage and Ignatius, and concludes that spiritual is not equivalent to immaterial or symbolic.
The immediate context of First Corinthians contrasts mortal flesh with spirit and does not support a physically transformed body.
This directly contests the pro side's interpretation of Paul's principal resurrection passage and therefore bears centrally on whether Paul taught bodily resurrection.
Albrecht's claim that Paul's use of spiritual does not mean immaterial or symbolic.
After Albrecht appeals to historical usage of the word spiritual, Price argues that immediate literary context controls and that Paul opposes flesh to spirit.
Paul's sequence from a body sown in dishonor to one raised in glory identifies the spiritual body as the same physical body transformed.
The move directly interprets a foundational early Christian source as teaching a tangible bodily resurrection, which is the proposition under debate.
Price's argument that Paul's immediate context opposes mortal flesh to spirit.
Albrecht answers Price by reading adjacent verses together, arguing that glory and spirituality describe transformation of a physical body rather than replacement by an immaterial entity.
Claims of apostolic succession and early institutional pedigree cannot be verified and resemble competing lineage claims in other religious traditions.
It attacks the reliability of the historical transmission chain on which Albrecht relies to connect later witnesses with the apostles and resurrection testimony.
Albrecht's claim that apostolic writers provide reliable historical references to an early belief.
Price argues that later communities had incentives to claim prestigious founders and that rival apostolic-lineage assertions cannot independently verify a historical chain.
Agreement among geographically and culturally separated early churches supports a common apostolic source for belief in Christ's bodily resurrection.
The argument offers independent convergence across early communities as historical support for apostolic origin rather than later coordinated fabrication.
Price's comparison of apostolic succession claims to unverifiable and competitive religious pedigrees.
Albrecht argues that separated Syriac, Latin, and Greek traditions teach the same bodily-resurrection belief despite lacking the coordination expected under a fabrication hypothesis.
Even granting a God capable of miracles does not establish that God performed every miracle attributed to him, including Jesus's resurrection.
The distinction between a miracle's possibility and its historical occurrence directly limits what theism alone can establish about the debated resurrection claim.
The suggestion that assuming a miracle-capable God should change the skeptical historical conclusion.
In the question period, Price accepts the hypothetical possibility of divine action while denying that possibility supplies evidence that this particular reported event occurred.
The apostles' identities, activities, and martyrdoms are too poorly known and too dependent on late legendary acts to support the resurrection argument.
This undercuts an important inference from apostolic preaching and martyrdom by disputing the historical premises that named apostles witnessed and died for the bodily resurrection.
The argument that known apostles preached bodily resurrection without gain and died as martyrs for it.
Price says apostolic lists vary, biographical information is sparse, and later acts contain conspicuously fantastic narratives, leaving insufficient historical grounding for martyrdom claims.
Extant writings and later catalogues attest real apostolic fathers independently of fanciful apocryphal stories and preserve early bodily-resurrection belief.
The move defends the existence and evidential relevance of Albrecht's principal post-apostolic witnesses against the charge that the case rests on legendary literature.
Price's claim that knowledge of the apostles and their deaths derives chiefly from fanciful late legends.
Albrecht points to writings attributed to identifiable early fathers, subsequent testimony to their existence, and cataloguing by Irenaeus and Jerome as a separate evidential stream.
Martyrdom shows sincere belief rather than truth, while Christianity's social practices and accessibility provide ordinary explanations for its rapid spread.
The response supplies alternative explanations for two major circumstantial arguments offered for resurrection: willingness to die and exceptional growth of the movement.
The argument that disciples' martyrdom, Paul's conversion, and rapid Christian growth support resurrection truth.

Price distinguishes courage from factual correctness, compares other sincere religious deaths, and attributes Christian growth to charity, demographics, missionary marriage, and appeal to God-fearing Gentiles.
Paul and early martyrs accepted persecution because they believed testimony to a physically risen Christ, unlike movements founded by demonstrable religious innovators.
The move defends costly conversion and martyrdom as grounded in bodily-resurrection testimony while resisting Price's analogy to sincere adherents of other religions.
Price's claim that martyrdom demonstrates sincerity only and is analogous to other religious believers.
Albrecht argues that Paul's abandonment of status and acceptance of persecution make sense as responses to resurrection testimony and denies equivalence with later religious founders.
Christianity expanded because converts encountered eyewitness-linked resurrection testimony and accepted a faith whose truth outweighed continuing persecution.
This directly counters naturalistic accounts of Christian growth by treating eyewitness contact, early resistance, conversion, and costly commitment as effects of resurrection truth.
Price's ordinary social and demographic explanation for Christianity's rapid early expansion.

Albrecht attributes growth to contact with witnesses, cites Justin and opposition to Christian texts, then argues that Christian worship and fulfilled expectations remained attractive despite martyrdom.
The examined pagan deities provide no testimony parallel to Jesus being crucified, dying, and bodily rising from the dead.
The claimed absence of pagan bodily-resurrection parallels directly supports the uniqueness of Jesus's resurrection against Price's historical-analogy case.
Price's earlier contention that Jesus and other ancient figures exhibit significant resurrection and savior parallels.
In his closing statement, Albrecht directly disputes Price's comparative mythology case after saying he has meticulously examined a list of proposed pagan analogues.
Justin Martyr treated Christ's death and resurrection as unique and portrayed pagan similarities as later imitations of Christianity.
The interpretation of Justin Martyr supplies a historical answer to the claim that Christianity borrowed its resurrection narrative from prior pagan traditions.
Price's use of Justin Martyr and ancient religious similarities to support pagan precedent or Christian borrowing.
Albrecht shifts from surveying named pagan figures to interpreting Justin Martyr, conceding some similarities while arguing they neither predate Christianity nor parallel bodily resurrection.
Early Greek usage distinguishes what is spiritual from what is immaterial, so a spiritual resurrection body need not be vaporous or nonphysical.
This linguistic distinction directly answers a nonbodily reading of resurrection language and supports interpreting the risen body as materially continuous rather than immaterial.
Price's earlier interpretation of spiritual resurrection language as evidence against a materially bodily resurrection.
Albrecht recommends a lexical study and invokes Cyril of Alexandria's contrasting Greek terms to argue that spiritual and immaterial were distinguishable concepts in early usage.
Paul transmits extensive testimony to Christ's bodily resurrection and presents what he received as revelation from the risen Lord.
The provenance and content of Paul's testimony bear directly on whether an early Christian source genuinely claimed that Jesus bodily rose from the dead.
Price's skeptical treatment of Paul's resurrection testimony and its basis, transmission, and bodily meaning.
As his principal takeaway, Albrecht appeals to Paul and other early followers, arguing that Paul's received-and-delivered testimony ultimately came from Christ rather than merely Peter.
John and Acts identify the raised temple as Jesus's body and proclaim that God raised the killed author of life bodily from the dead.
These cited early Christian texts explicitly connect resurrection with Jesus's body, directly affirming the precise bodily-resurrection claim posed by the motion.
In his final seconds, Albrecht condenses his affirmative case into passages from John and Acts that describe Jesus's body as the temple raised after three days.
Specialist literature documents numerous parallels between Jesus and a range of other ancient religious figures.
The cited body of comparative evidence supports Price's historical-analogy skepticism and directly contests Albrecht's claim that relevant pagan parallels are absent.
Albrecht's closing assertion that meticulous examination reveals no meaningful pagan parallels to Jesus's resurrection narrative.
Rather than repeat his full case, Price recommends a work by M. David Litwa and characterizes it as presenting a large body of ancient parallels involving Jesus.
